questions.stem: What was the zollverein? State two ways in which it helped the economic unification of the German states.
questions.answer: The zollverein was a customs union formed in 1834 at the initiative of Prussia and joined by most of the German states. It abolished tariff barriers and reduced the number of currencies from over thirty to two, allowing freer movement of goods and capital.

questions.stem: How did the clergy in Poland use language as a weapon of national resistance against Russian rule?
questions.answer: After Russian occupation the Polish language was forced out of schools and Russian was imposed everywhere. After the failed armed rebellion of 1831, many members of the clergy used Polish for Church gatherings and all religious instruction. Many priests and bishops were jailed or sent to Siberia for refusing to preach in Russian, and the use of Polish came to be seen as a symbol of the struggle against Russian dominance.

questions.stem: Who was the architect of German unification? How was the unification completed, and where was the German Empire proclaimed?
questions.answer: Otto von Bismarck, the chief minister of Prussia, was the architect of German unification, carried out with the help of the Prussian army and bureaucracy. Three wars over seven years — with Austria, Denmark and France — ended in Prussian victory and completed unification. In January 1871 the Prussian king William I was proclaimed German Emperor in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles.

questions.stem: What changes did Napoleon introduce to make the administrative system more efficient in the territories ruled by him? Why did the local populations later turn hostile to French rule?
questions.answer: The Civil Code of 1804 (Napoleonic Code) did away with privileges based on birth, established equality before the law and secured the right to property. In the Dutch Republic, Switzerland, Italy and Germany he simplified administrative divisions, abolished the feudal system and freed peasants from serfdom and manorial dues; guild restrictions in towns were removed and transport and communication were improved. The initial enthusiasm turned to hostility because the new arrangements did not go with political freedom: increased taxation, censorship and forced conscription into the French armies outweighed the advantages.
valuePoints: Civil Code of 1804: no privileges by birth, equality before law, right to property
Simplified administrative divisions, abolished feudal system, freed peasants from serfdom and manorial dues, removed guild restrictions, improved transport and communication
Hostility because of increased taxation, censorship, forced conscription and no political freedom

questions.stem: Give three examples to show how culture contributed to the growth of nationalism in Europe.
questions.answer: (1) Romantic thinkers such as Johann Gottfried Herder held that true German culture was found among the common people (das volk); folk songs, folk poetry and folk dances popularised the spirit of the nation (volksgeist). (2) The Grimm brothers collected folktales, published in 1812, which they saw as the pure German spirit, and saw their work as part of the effort to oppose French domination and create a German national identity. (3) In partitioned Poland, national feeling was kept alive through music and language: Karol Kurpinski turned folk dances like the polonaise and mazurka into nationalist symbols. (Also acceptable: Delacroix's Massacre at Chios creating sympathy for the Greeks.)
valuePoints: Herder and the idea of das volk / volksgeist through folk culture
Grimm brothers' folktales as part of opposing French domination
Poland: Kurpinski's operas and music; polonaise and mazurka as nationalist symbols

questions.stem: 'Equality before the law did not necessarily stand for universal suffrage.' Explain this statement with reference to the liberal movement in Europe.
questions.answer: In revolutionary France the right to vote and to be elected was granted only to property-owning men; men without property and all women were excluded, and only briefly under the Jacobins did all adult males vote. The Napoleonic Code went back to limited suffrage and reduced women to the status of a minor, subject to fathers and husbands. In 1848, although women had formed political associations, founded newspapers and taken part in demonstrations, they were denied suffrage in the election of the Frankfurt Assembly and were admitted only as observers in the visitors' gallery.

questions.stem: Describe the process by which Italy was unified. Mention the roles of Mazzini, Cavour and Garibaldi.
questions.answer: In the mid-nineteenth century Italy was divided into seven states; only Sardinia-Piedmont was ruled by an Italian princely house, the north was under the Austrian Habsburgs, the centre under the Pope and the south under the Bourbon kings of Spain. During the 1830s Giuseppe Mazzini sought a coherent programme for a unitary Italian Republic and formed the secret society Young Italy. After the uprisings of 1831 and 1848 failed, the task fell to Sardinia-Piedmont under King Victor Emmanuel II. Chief Minister Cavour engineered a diplomatic alliance with France, and Sardinia-Piedmont defeated the Austrian forces in 1859. Armed volunteers under Giuseppe Garibaldi marched into South Italy and the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies in 1860 and won the support of local peasants to drive out the Spanish rulers. In 1861 Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed king of united Italy. The Papal States joined in 1870 when France withdrew its troops from Rome during its war with Prussia.

Cavour: alliance with France; Austria defeated in 1859

questions.stem: Why did the Balkans become the most serious source of nationalist tension in Europe after 1871? How did nationalism become linked with imperialism?
questions.answer: The Balkans was a region of geographical and ethnic variation (modern-day Romania, Bulgaria, Albania, Greece, Macedonia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Slovenia, Serbia and Montenegro) whose inhabitants were broadly known as Slavs, and a large part of it was under the Ottoman Empire. The spread of romantic nationalism together with the disintegration of the Ottoman Empire made it explosive; one by one its European subject nationalities broke away and declared independence. The Balkan peoples used history to claim they had once been independent, so they saw their struggles as winning back long-lost independence. The Balkan states were fiercely jealous of each other and each hoped to gain territory at the others' expense. The area also became the scene of big power rivalry: Russia, Germany, England and Austro-Hungary each wanted to counter the others' hold and extend its own control. By the last quarter of the nineteenth century nationalism had become a narrow creed, and the major powers manipulated the nationalist aspirations of subject peoples for their own imperialist aims. This led to a series of wars and finally the First World War — nationalism aligned with imperialism led Europe to disaster in 1914.
valuePoints: Ethnically varied region of Slavs, largely under the Ottoman Empire
Romantic nationalism plus disintegration of the Ottoman Empire made it explosive
Balkan states jealous of each other, each wanting more territory
Big power rivalry: Russia, Germany, England, Austro-Hungary
Powers manipulated nationalism for imperialist aims, leading to the First World War

questions.passage: Each of these possessed its own currency, and weights and measures. A merchant travelling in 1833 from Hamburg to Nuremberg to sell his goods would have had to pass through 11 customs barriers and pay a customs duty of about 5 per cent at each one of them. Duties were often levied according to the weight or measurement of the goods. As each region had its own system of weights and measures, this involved time-consuming calculation. The measure of cloth, for example, was the elle which in each region stood for a different length. An elle of textile material bought in Frankfurt would get you 54.7 cm of cloth, in Mainz 55.1 cm, in Nuremberg 65.6 cm, in Freiburg 53.5 cm.

questions.reason: The Rowlatt Act gave the government enormous powers to repress political activities and allowed detention of political prisoners without trial for two years.

questions.stem: What happened at Jallianwalla Bagh on 13 April 1919?
questions.answer: A large crowd gathered in the enclosed ground of Jallianwalla Bagh — some to protest against the government's new repressive measures, others to attend the annual Baisakhi fair; many villagers did not know martial law had been imposed. General Dyer entered, blocked the exit points and opened fire on the crowd, killing hundreds. His object, he declared later, was to 'produce a moral effect' — terror and awe in the minds of satyagrahis.

questions.stem: How did the Non-Cooperation Movement unfold in the towns, and why did it gradually slow down there?
questions.answer: Thousands of students left government-controlled schools and colleges, headmasters and teachers resigned, lawyers gave up practice, and council elections were boycotted in most provinces except Madras. Foreign goods were boycotted, liquor shops picketed and foreign cloth burnt; imports of foreign cloth halved between 1921 and 1922, from Rs 102 crore to Rs 57 crore. It slowed down because khadi was often more expensive than mass-produced mill cloth and the poor could not afford it, and alternative Indian institutions were slow to come up, so students, teachers and lawyers trickled back.

questions.stem: How did the tribal peasants of the Gudem Hills in Andhra Pradesh interpret the message of Mahatma Gandhi and the idea of swaraj?
questions.answer: The colonial government had closed large forest areas, stopping people from grazing cattle or collecting fuelwood and fruits, and then forced them to contribute begar for road building, so the hill people revolted. They were led by Alluri Sitaram Raju, who spoke of Gandhiji's greatness, said he was inspired by the Non-Cooperation Movement and persuaded people to wear khadi and give up drinking — but asserted that India could be liberated only by force, not non-violence. The rebels attacked police stations, attempted to kill British officials and carried on guerrilla warfare for swaraj; Raju was captured and executed in 1924.

questions.stem: Explain how the image of Bharat Mata and the revival of folklore helped create a sense of collective belonging in India.
questions.answer: The image of Bharat Mata was first created by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay, who wrote 'Vande Mataram' in the 1870s as a hymn to the motherland; it was included in Anandamath and widely sung in the Swadeshi movement. Abanindranath Tagore painted Bharat Mata as a calm, divine, ascetic figure, and devotion to this mother figure came to be seen as evidence of one's nationalism. Nationalists also recorded folk tales, songs and legends, believing they gave a true picture of traditional culture; Rabindranath Tagore collected ballads, nursery rhymes and myths, and Natesa Sastri published The Folklore of Southern India.

questions.stem: Why did different social groups join the Civil Disobedience Movement? Explain with reference to rich peasants, poor peasants, business classes, industrial workers and women.
questions.answer: Rich peasants such as the Patidars of Gujarat and the Jats of Uttar Pradesh, producers of commercial crops, were hard hit by the depression and falling prices and could not pay revenue; for them swaraj meant a struggle against high revenues. Poorer peasants, many of them small tenants, wanted unpaid rent to the landlord remitted and joined radical movements, but the Congress was unwilling to support 'no rent' campaigns. Business classes, organised in FICCI (1927) and led by Purshottamdas Thakurdas and G. D. Birla, wanted protection against foreign imports and supported the movement when it was launched, seeing swaraj as the end of colonial restrictions on business. Industrial workers did not join in large numbers except in the Nagpur region, though some adopted boycott and there were railway (1930) and dock (1932) strikes. Women joined in large numbers — marching, manufacturing salt, picketing foreign cloth and liquor shops — seeing service to the nation as a sacred duty.
valuePoints: Rich peasants: hit by falling prices; against high revenue demand
Poor peasants: wanted rent remitted; Congress would not back 'no rent' campaigns
Business classes: wanted protection against imports; FICCI; financial support
Workers: limited participation except Nagpur; some strikes and boycotts
Women: large-scale participation in marches, salt making and picketing

questions.stem: Explain the limits of the Civil Disobedience Movement with reference to the dalits and the Muslims.
questions.answer: Dalits: for long the Congress had ignored them for fear of offending the conservative high-caste sanatanis. Gandhiji called them harijan and organised satyagraha for temple entry and access to public wells, tanks, roads and schools, but many dalit leaders wanted a political solution — reserved seats in educational institutions and separate electorates. Dr B.R. Ambedkar, who organised the Depressed Classes Association in 1930, clashed with Gandhiji at the second Round Table Conference over separate electorates; Gandhiji's fast unto death led to the Poona Pact of September 1932, giving reserved seats to be voted in by the general electorate. Dalit participation stayed limited, especially in Maharashtra and Nagpur. Muslims: after the decline of the Non-Cooperation-Khilafat Movement many felt alienated from the Congress, which from the mid-1920s was associated with groups like the Hindu Mahasabha; communal clashes widened the distance. Efforts at an alliance failed at the All Parties Conference in 1928 when M.R. Jayakar opposed compromise with Jinnah's proposals, and many Muslims feared their culture and identity would be submerged under a Hindu majority.
valuePoints: Congress had ignored dalits for fear of offending sanatanis; dalit leaders sought reserved seats and separate electorates
Ambedkar's clash with Gandhiji; fast unto death; Poona Pact 1932
Muslims alienated after the Khilafat movement's decline; association with Hindu Mahasabha; communal riots
Failure of negotiations in 1928 (Jinnah's proposals, Jayakar's opposition)
Fear of minority culture being submerged under a Hindu majority

questions.passage: Mahatma Gandhi found in salt a powerful symbol that could unite the nation. On 31 January 1930, he sent a letter to Viceroy Irwin stating eleven demands. Some of these were of general interest; others were specific demands of different classes, from industrialists to peasants. The idea was to make the demands wide-ranging, so that all classes within Indian society could identify with them and everyone could be brought together in a united campaign. The most stirring of all was the demand to abolish the salt tax. Salt was something consumed by the rich and the poor alike, and it was one of the most essential items of food. The tax on salt and the government monopoly over its production, Mahatma Gandhi declared, revealed the most oppressive face of British rule.

questions.stem: Explain how the centre of world trade moved westwards to Europe.
questions.answer: Until well into the eighteenth century China and India were among the world's richest countries and pre-eminent in Asian trade. However, from the fifteenth century China is said to have restricted overseas contacts and retreated into isolation. China's reduced role and the rising importance of the Americas — whose lands, crops and minerals, especially silver, transformed trade — gradually moved the centre of world trade westwards, and Europe emerged as the centre of world trade.

questions.stem: 'The making of the global world has a long history.' Support this statement with five examples of links between societies in the pre-modern world.
questions.answer: (1) As early as 3000 BCE an active coastal trade linked the Indus valley civilisations with present-day West Asia. (2) For more than a millennium, cowries from the Maldives, used as currency, found their way to China and East Africa. (3) The long-distance spread of disease-carrying germs can be traced to the seventh century and was an unmistakable link by the thirteenth. (4) The silk routes, existing since before the Christian Era, linked Asia with Europe and northern Africa, carrying silk, pottery, spices, gold and silver as well as missionaries, preachers and Buddhism. (5) Food travelled: noodles are believed to have travelled west from China to become spaghetti, or Arab traders took pasta to fifth-century Sicily. (Also acceptable: the Indian Ocean's bustling trade with the Indian subcontinent at its centre.)
valuePoints: Indus valley coastal trade with West Asia, 3000 BCE
Maldives cowries reaching China and East Africa
Spread of germs from the seventh century
Silk routes linking Asia, Europe and northern Africa
Food exchanges such as noodles and spaghetti; Indian Ocean trade

questions.stem: Explain what we mean when we say that the world 'shrank' in the sixteenth century. How did the discovery of America transform trade and lives?
questions.answer: The pre-modern world shrank greatly in the sixteenth century after European sailors found a sea route to Asia and also crossed the western ocean to America. The Indian Ocean had long known a bustling trade with the Indian subcontinent at its centre; the entry of the Europeans expanded or redirected some of these flows towards Europe. America, cut off from regular contact with the rest of the world for millions of years, now saw its vast lands, abundant crops and minerals transform trade and lives everywhere. Silver from mines in present-day Peru and Mexico enhanced Europe's wealth and financed its trade with Asia, and expeditions set off in search of El Dorado, the fabled city of gold. The Portuguese and Spanish conquest was under way by the mid-sixteenth century, helped above all by germs such as smallpox, to which the original inhabitants had no immunity. New crops such as potatoes and maize reached Europe and Asia, and by the eighteenth century plantations worked by African slaves grew cotton and sugar for European markets.
valuePoints: European sailors found a sea route to Asia and crossed to America
Indian Ocean flows expanded or redirected towards Europe
American silver enhanced Europe's wealth and financed trade with Asia; El Dorado
Conquest aided by smallpox; no immunity among original inhabitants
New crops spread; slave plantations growing cotton and sugar

questions.passage: The Portuguese and Spanish conquest and colonisation of America was decisively under way by the mid-sixteenth century. European conquest was not just a result of superior firepower. In fact, the most powerful weapon of the Spanish conquerors was not a conventional military weapon at all. It was the germs such as those of smallpox that they carried on their person. Because of their long isolation, America's original inhabitants had no immunity against these diseases that came from Europe. Smallpox in particular proved a deadly killer. Once introduced, it spread deep into the continent, ahead even of any Europeans reaching there. It killed and decimated whole communities, paving the way for conquest.

questions.stem: How were books printed in China from AD 594 onwards? Why was the traditional Chinese book folded as an 'accordion book'?
questions.answer: Books were printed by rubbing paper against the inked surface of woodblocks — a system of hand printing. As both sides of the thin, porous sheet could not be printed, the accordion book was folded and stitched at the side.

questions.stem: When and how did the printing press first come to India? What did the missionaries print?
questions.answer: The printing press first came to Goa with Portuguese missionaries in the mid-sixteenth century. Jesuit priests learnt Konkani and printed several tracts; by 1674 about 50 books had been printed in the Konkani and Kanara languages. Catholic priests printed the first Tamil book in 1579 at Cochin.

questions.stem: How did print help to raise questions of caste discrimination in India? Give two examples.
questions.answer: From the late nineteenth century, caste discrimination was written about in many printed tracts and essays. Jyotiba Phule, the Maratha pioneer of 'low caste' protest movements, wrote about the injustices of the caste system in Gulamgiri (1871). In the twentieth century B.R. Ambedkar in Maharashtra and E.V. Ramaswamy Naicker (Periyar) in Madras wrote powerfully on caste and were read all over India. Kashibaba, a Kanpur millworker, published Chhote Aur Bade Ka Sawal in 1938 on the links between caste and class exploitation.
valuePoints: Jyotiba Phule's Gulamgiri (1871)
Ambedkar and Periyar wrote powerfully on caste
Kashibaba's Chhote Aur Bade Ka Sawal (1938)

questions.stem: Why was Martin Luther in favour of print? How did print help bring about the Protestant Reformation?
questions.answer: In 1517 Luther wrote the Ninety Five Theses criticising many practices and rituals of the Roman Catholic Church, and a printed copy was posted on a church door in Wittenberg. His writings were immediately reproduced in vast numbers and read widely, which led to a division within the Church and the beginning of the Protestant Reformation. His translation of the New Testament sold 5,000 copies within a few weeks and a second edition appeared within three months. Deeply grateful, Luther said, 'Printing is the ultimate gift of God and the greatest one.'
valuePoints: Ninety Five Theses (1517) criticising the Church; posted in Wittenberg
Writings reproduced in vast numbers; division in the Church; Reformation began
New Testament sold 5,000 copies in weeks; Luther called printing the ultimate gift of God

questions.stem: Why do some historians think that print culture created the conditions within which the French Revolution occurred? Give three arguments.
questions.answer: First, print popularised the ideas of Enlightenment thinkers such as Voltaire and Rousseau, who argued for the rule of reason rather than custom and attacked the sacred authority of the Church and the despotic power of the state. Second, print created a new culture of dialogue and debate in which all values, norms and institutions were re-evaluated by a public aware of the power of reason. Third, by the 1780s there was an outpouring of literature, cartoons and caricatures that mocked royalty and criticised its morality, which circulated underground and led to hostile sentiments against the monarchy.

Created a culture of dialogue and debate
Literature and cartoons of the 1780s mocking royalty spread hostility to the monarchy

questions.stem: How did print shape religious reform and public debate in nineteenth-century India? Give three examples.
questions.answer: In Bengal, reformers and the Hindu orthodoxy debated widow immolation, monotheism, Brahmanical priesthood and idolatry in tracts and newspapers printed in everyday spoken language: Rammohun Roy published the Sambad Kaumudi from 1821 and the orthodoxy commissioned the Samachar Chandrika to oppose him. In north India the ulama used cheap lithographic presses to publish Persian and Urdu translations of scriptures, and the Deoband Seminary (founded 1867) published thousands of fatwas. Among Hindus, the first printed edition of Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas came out from Calcutta in 1810, and from the 1880s the Naval Kishore Press at Lucknow and the Shri Venkateshwar Press in Bombay published religious texts in vernaculars that could be read out to illiterate people.

Ulama and the Deoband Seminary's fatwas using lithographic presses

questions.stem: What did the spread of print culture in nineteenth-century India mean to women? Explain with examples.
questions.answer: Lives and feelings of women began to be written about vividly, and women's reading increased enormously in middle-class homes; liberal husbands and fathers educated women at home and sent them to schools set up after the mid-nineteenth century. Journals carried writings by women, explained why women should be educated, and gave a syllabus for home-based schooling. Not all families were liberal: conservative Hindus believed a literate girl would be widowed and Muslims feared Urdu romances would corrupt women, but some women defied this — Rashsundari Debi learnt to read secretly in her kitchen and wrote Amar Jiban (1876), the first full-length autobiography in Bengali. Women wrote about their own lives: Kailashbashini Debi from the 1860s, and Tarabai Shinde and Pandita Ramabai in the 1880s wrote about the miserable lives of upper-caste Hindu women, especially widows. In the early twentieth century, journals written for and sometimes edited by women discussed women's education, widowhood, widow remarriage and the national movement, and Battala publications were carried by pedlars to homes for women to read.

questions.stem: Describe how Gutenberg developed the printing press, and how printing spread in Europe between 1450 and 1550.
questions.answer: Gutenberg, the son of a merchant, grew up on a large agricultural estate and had seen wine and olive presses from childhood; he became a master goldsmith and learnt to create lead moulds for making trinkets. Drawing on this, he adapted existing technology: the olive press was the model for the printing press, and moulds were used to cast metal types for the letters of the alphabet. By 1448 he perfected the system, and the first book he printed was the Bible — about 180 copies in three years, fast by the standards of the time. At first printed books closely resembled manuscripts: metal letters imitated ornamental handwriting and borders were illuminated by hand. Between 1450 and 1550 printing presses were set up in most countries of Europe, as printers from Germany travelled to other countries seeking work; about 20 million copies of printed books flooded Europe's markets in the second half of the fifteenth century, rising to about 200 million in the sixteenth. This shift from hand printing to mechanical printing led to the print revolution.

questions.passage: After the revolt of 1857, the attitude to freedom of the press changed. Enraged Englishmen demanded a clamp down on the 'native' press. As vernacular newspapers became assertively nationalist, the colonial government began debating measures of stringent control. In 1878, the Vernacular Press Act was passed, modelled on the Irish Press Laws. It provided the government with extensive rights to censor reports and editorials in the vernacular press. From now on the government kept regular track of the vernacular newspapers published in different provinces. When a report was judged as seditious, the newspaper was warned, and if the warning was ignored, the press was liable to be seized and the printing machinery confiscated.

parts.prompt: The Vernacular Press Act of 1878 was modelled on which laws?

parts.answer: The press was liable to be seized and the printing machinery confiscated.

parts.prompt: Despite such repressive measures, how did nationalist newspapers respond? Give one example from the chapter.
parts.answer: Nationalist newspapers grew in numbers in all parts of India, reported on colonial misrule and encouraged nationalist activities (1 mark). Example: when Punjab revolutionaries were deported in 1907, Balgangadhar Tilak wrote with great sympathy about them in his Kesari, which led to his imprisonment in 1908 and widespread protests (1 mark).
